# Researchfish: What It Is and Why UK Research Funders Require It

Researchfish is the outcomes-reporting platform UKRI, NIHR, and other UK funders use for mandatory grant reporting — what it is, the annual reporting obligation, what gets reported, and its planned 2027 closure.

Written and maintained by <a href="/about/editorial-policy" class="font-medium text-foreground hover:text-primary hover:underline">CASRAI Editorial Board</a>

Published 17 July 2026 · Last updated 24 August 2026

Researchfish is an online research-outcomes reporting platform, not a citation-discovery  
or literature-search tool. Grant holders use it to submit self-reported outcomes —  
publications, collaborations, further funding, commercial and policy impact, and more —  
against specific funded awards, and research funders use the aggregated returns to track  
what their money produced. It is the mechanism most UK research administrators mean when  
they talk about “reporting to UKRI” or “doing my Researchfish return.”

As of mid-2026, Researchfish is also in a genuinely unusual position: its owner, Elsevier,  
announced on 30 January 2026 that it will close the platform on 31 July 2027. The reporting  
obligation to funders isn’t going away, but the platform used to fulfil it is a confirmed  
moving target for the next year — this guide covers both the obligation as it stands today  
and what’s known about the transition ahead.

## What Researchfish is (and isn’t)

Researchfish began as a Medical Research Council (MRC) project in 2008, was taken on by  
the higher-education software company Interfolio in 2019, and was acquired by the academic  
publisher Elsevier in 2022, which markets it today as part of its research-intelligence  
product line alongside Scopus and SciVal. Functionally, it’s a submission portal:  
researchers create an account, connect it to their funded awards, and enter outcome data  
against a standard set of questions once a year (with the option to update continuously).

It is easy to confuse with tools covered elsewhere on this site that also touch a  
researcher’s output record — [ORCID](/dictionary/term/orcid-id), a  
[CRIS/RIM platform](/pillar/cris-identifiers), or a literature-discovery tool like  
Semantic Scholar or OpenAlex — but the function is different. Those tools help someone find,  
identify, or cross-reference research and researchers. Researchfish exists specifically so a  
funder can ask “what did this grant actually produce?” and get a structured, comparable  
answer across an entire portfolio of awards.

## Which funders require Researchfish reporting

Researchfish is used by more than 90 research funders, most of them UK-based. The  
largest and most consequential for UK research administrators are:

- **UK Research and Innovation (UKRI)** — across its constituent research  
  councils, the primary funder driving Researchfish’s scale in UK higher education.
- **National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR)** — operates its  
  own sanctions policy alongside UKRI’s.
- **Cancer Research UK** — withholds grant payments to the host institution  
  for a missed or invalid submission.
- **Wellcome Trust** — used Researchfish through the 2025/26 submission  
  round (closing March 2026) but has announced it will not continue using the platform beyond  
  that point (see below).
- Other funders including the British Heart Foundation, the British Council, and a range  
  of medical research charities and international funders.

A deliberate design feature of the platform is that a researcher enters an output once  
and can attribute it to every relevant grant from every funder that uses Researchfish,  
rather than re-entering the same publication or collaboration separately for each funder’s  
own system.

See also [Health Data Research Service](/guides/health-data-research-service) — What the UK Health Data Research Service (HDRS) is, where it came from, what it will provide, how it is funded and governed, and how it differs from HDR UK.

## The grantee reporting obligation

For UKRI awards specifically, submitting an annual outcomes update is normally a  
condition written into the grant or fellowship’s terms and conditions, not an optional  
courtesy. The obligation falls on the named lead researcher (principal investigator), runs  
“from early in your project until at least five years after it ends,” and is collected  
during an annual submission window — for example, UKRI’s 2026 window ran from 2 February to  
12 March 2026. Outside the formal window, researchers can still update their record  
continuously.

Non-compliance carries real consequences, not just a reminder email. Per UKRI’s own  
published guidance, a researcher who misses their Researchfish submission:

- becomes ineligible to be named as Principal Investigator or Co-Investigator on any  
  further UKRI award, across every UKRI council, until all outstanding submissions are made;  
  and
- if the award in question is still active, has payments on that award withheld until an  
  up-to-date outcomes record is submitted.

NIHR and Cancer Research UK operate comparable sanctions policies — CRUK withholds  
institutional payments for a missing or invalid return, and NIHR can render a PI ineligible  
for further funding — though each funder’s exact policy and exemption criteria should be  
checked directly rather than assumed to match UKRI’s.

## What gets reported: the Common Question Set

The UK research councils harmonised their outcome-reporting questions into a shared  
framework generally referred to as the **Common Question Set** — reportedly  
around 16 main outcome categories broken into roughly 103 sub-types, applied consistently  
across disciplines so a funder can compare returns from an engineering grant and a medical  
humanities grant on the same structure. The main categories a grant holder is asked about  
include:

- **Publications** — journal articles, books, and other scholarly outputs,  
  increasingly harvested automatically from connected repositories rather than entered by  
  hand.
- **Collaborations and partnerships** — formal and informal research  
  relationships that arose from the funded work.
- **Further funding** — follow-on grants or awards secured on the strength of  
  the funded project.
- **Engagement activities / Public Engagement and Involvement (PE&I)** —  
  public- and patient-facing dissemination and involvement work.
- **Influence on policy, practice, patients, and the public** — evidence of  
  the research shaping decisions or services outside academia.
- **IP and licensing, and spin-outs** — commercialisation outcomes; UKRI’s  
  spin-out reporting now aligns to the UK Spinout Register’s definition.
- **Products, research tools and methods, and artistic or creative outputs**  
  — tangible outputs beyond a conventional publication.
- **Researcher and staff development, and next destination** — the training  
  and career outcomes for people employed on the grant.

Every outcome category also carries a free-text field for an **impact  
narrative** — the researcher’s own account of why a given output or collaboration  
mattered, in plain language rather than a metric. UKRI ran a reporting-burden review across  
2025 into 2026 that trimmed and reorganised parts of this question set (for example,  
folding “Awards and recognition” and “Use of facilities and resources” out of mandatory  
reporting and restructuring public engagement into a dedicated ten-question section) — the  
exact question set a grant holder sees can shift year to year, so it’s worth re-reading the  
current guidance rather than relying on a prior year’s form from memory.

## Why funders use aggregated Researchfish data

A single funder like UKRI runs thousands of active grants at once. Researchfish exists  
because asking each grant holder individually, in whatever format they choose, doesn’t  
scale into anything a funder can analyse, compare, or report upward. Aggregating structured  
returns across a whole portfolio lets a funder:

- assess the outcomes and impact of its investment at a **portfolio level** —  
  across a whole scheme, discipline, or funding call, not just one grant at a time;
- meet its own accountability obligations to government, donors, or trustees — UKRI’s  
  figures describe funders collectively reporting on tens of billions of pounds in funding to  
  government and other stakeholders using Researchfish-sourced data;
- publish outcome information openly — for UKRI-funded work, submitted outcomes surface  
  publicly through <a href="https://gtr.ukri.org" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Gateway to<br />
  Research</a>, UKRI’s public database of funded projects and their outputs.

Researchfish data has also fed into academic research on research assessment itself — a  
published proof-of-concept study linked [REF  
impact case studies](/dictionary/term/impact-case-study-ref) from the 2014 Research Excellence Framework to the underpinning  
grants recorded in Researchfish, matching primarily via publication identifiers, to explore  
which funding characteristics correlate with impact case studies. It’s worth being precise  
about what this does and doesn’t mean: Researchfish is not itself part of the official REF  
submission mechanism (impact case studies are submitted separately by institutions to  
Research England), but its portfolio-level data has proven useful as an analytical resource  
for understanding how funded research translates into recognised impact. See CASRAI’s  
dictionary entries on [pathway to impact](/dictionary/term/pathway-to-impact) and  
[impact evaluation](/dictionary/term/impact-evaluation) for the broader vocabulary  
this connects to.

## Researchfish’s planned closure: what grant holders need to know

On 30 January 2026, Elsevier announced it will sunset Researchfish on 31 July 2027,  
saying the move lets it “focus on solutions that better align with customers’ needs.” The  
platform had faced years of researcher criticism over its usability — a 2024 UK government  
review of research bureaucracy described it as “burdensome for users” and said it “does not  
make the best use of recent technological advances.” Elsevier states the platform will  
remain fully supported and operational until the closure date, with data retained for 12  
months after each individual funder’s contract with Researchfish ends.

The timing is notable: UKRI renewed its own Researchfish contract, following a  
competitive tender that reportedly found no viable alternative at the time, only months  
before the closure was announced. That leaves UKRI and Researchfish’s other 90-plus funders  
with a defined but tight window — commentary in the sector has described it as roughly 18  
months from the announcement to close — to agree on and build a replacement, individually or  
collectively, before mid-2027.

Wellcome Trust reached its own decision independently: it will not use Researchfish  
beyond the 2025/26 submission round (which closed in March 2026) and is developing its own  
outcomes-reporting tool instead. As of mid-2026, no confirmed successor system has been  
announced by UKRI or most of the other affected funders.

**What this means practically, right now:** the underlying obligation to  
report your outcomes to your funder has not changed and shouldn’t be treated as suspended —  
continue meeting your current Researchfish submission windows exactly as before. What’s  
worth watching over the next 12–18 months is your specific funder’s own communications about  
a successor platform, since the transition (if it happens funder-by-funder rather than  
through a shared solution) could mean re-entering historical outcome data into a new system.  
Keeping your own independent record of what you’ve reported — beyond what Researchfish  
itself retains — is a reasonable precaution given the confirmed data-deletion policy after a  
funder’s contract ends.

## Practical guidance for grant holders and research administrators

- **Know your submission window.** It’s set annually by the platform/funder  
  combination and can move year to year (UKRI’s 2026 window closed 12 March 2026) — check  
  current guidance rather than assuming last year’s dates.
- **Use the “report once” design deliberately.** If more than one of your  
  funders uses Researchfish, a single entered output can be attributed to every relevant  
  grant rather than re-keyed per funder.
- **Track your funder’s specific sanctions policy.** UKRI, NIHR, and Cancer  
  Research UK each publish their own — the consequences (payment withholding, PI ineligibility)  
  are broadly similar but not identical, and eligibility exemptions differ.
- **Keep independent records.** Don’t rely on Researchfish as your  
  institution’s permanent archive of reported outcomes, particularly with a confirmed closure  
  date on the calendar and a 12-month post-contract data-deletion policy already in place.
- **Watch for successor-platform announcements** from your specific funders  
  between now and July 2027, rather than assuming continuity with the current system.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Researchfish mandatory?

For UKRI grant and fellowship holders, yes — annual outcomes reporting via Researchfish  
is normally a condition of the award’s terms and conditions, unless the researcher holds a  
specific exemption. Many other funders that use Researchfish, including NIHR and Cancer  
Research UK, treat it as mandatory too, each under its own sanctions policy.

### What happens if I don’t submit my Researchfish return?

For UKRI awards, a missed submission makes the named lead researcher ineligible to be PI  
or Co-I on any further UKRI award, across all UKRI councils, until every outstanding  
submission is made — and if the current award is still active, payments on it can be  
withheld until the outcomes record is up to date. Other funders that use Researchfish apply  
comparable sanctions.

### How long after my grant ends do I have to keep reporting?

For UKRI awards, the obligation runs from early in the project until at least five years  
after the award ends.

### Is Researchfish closing?

Yes. Elsevier announced on 30 January 2026 that it will close Researchfish on 31 July  
2027. The platform remains fully operational and supported until that date, but funders —  
including UKRI, which had recently renewed its contract — are now working out what replaces  
it.

### Does Wellcome Trust still use Researchfish?

Wellcome used Researchfish through its 2025/26 submission round, which closed in March  
2026, and has said it will not continue using the platform beyond that point, opting instead  
to develop its own reporting tool.

### Is Researchfish the same as ORCID or a CRIS?

No. [ORCID](/dictionary/term/orcid-id) is a persistent identifier for an  
individual researcher; a [CRIS/RIM platform](/pillar/cris-identifiers) is  
institutional infrastructure for managing research information generally. Researchfish is  
narrower and funder-facing: a reporting portal a grant holder uses specifically to tell a  
funder what a particular funded award produced. An institution’s CRIS may separately import  
or reference Researchfish outcome data, but the two systems serve different primary  
purposes.
